doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: His son's musical life
summary: Griffin talks about his son's early musicianship, the divorce, Teaneck, a summer band, and his son's Broadway work.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: Were you pleased that your son pursued the music business?

Yes. Believe it or not it was a weird kind of situation with my son. His mother passed two years ago and my former wife, I never married, we got a divorce kind of early in my son’s life but I never re-married. But he was always into music. Okay I’ll give you an example about him. At two years old he could play the piano and he would go [scats] “Popcorn” he had a song. He wrote all these songs. “Peanuts” and everything [scats] “Popcorn” [scats] so he was composing way back then, and then when I was playing the trombone he would come in and he could play the trombone. He could hold it up and play it but he could only get to fourth position. So I figured out okay he probably needs to play the trumpet because then at least he won’t have to have the arm reach thing. And then that was when we were living in Manhattan at 70 West 95th Street. Then we moved to Teaneck when he went to the first grade. So he stayed in music up until junior high he was getting ready to go to junior high school and I got a divorce, me and his mother divorced. But I stayed in Teaneck so I could be a part of his life and everything, and oh he was winning band contests during those times, the state band and everything. And in © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

the summer I had the honor of, this was a friend of Ed Pasant. He’s not with us anymore. His daughter played the clarinet and Ed played the clarinet, and they would have a summer band with the parents and I would play trombone and my son would be playing the percussion and everything, and that was really, really nice. So my son, he never had like a day job, you know like kids wanted to work, you know at 7-Eleven or all these different stores, my son was the only child, so he got a job at 7-Eleven, and he was there for a couple of weeks. He didn’t know how to hold the broom to sweep, because he had never done it. He never had to do it. He was an only child you know, and his mother did everything for him, so he didn’t know how to sweep the floor or how to clean up and do everything. I would go watch. And I’d park my car like in a second where I could just watch him. And I would just be laughing, I’d say that boy, I’ve got to show him how to hold a broom and how to sweep and everything. That job lasted about two weeks and that was the only job I think I ever remember him having other than playing music.
Yes and we’ve had the pleasure of his talents here at Hamilton College a number of times.

Oh yeah. Yeah. He comes up, he used to come up annually and would play with Doctor Woods. But yeah, so now he’s 53 years old, he’s never had a job doing anything but playing music. And he got to be pretty good — well he is pretty good I’ve got to say. He reads very well. He plays all styles, like I do. He just subbed in a Broadway show at the Wintergarden Theater, a really really big show there and he did pretty good there. And he said coming up March 1 he’s going to be doing “Dream Girls,” it’s going to be a three week run, which is like a Broadway — one of the big shows of Broadway. So I’m proud of him and he’s doing well and never done anything but music.
That is really something in this day and age.
